transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-11-04 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Avery Lin (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (HorizonBridge CTO), Priya Banerjee (HorizonBridge Eng Manager), Sam Ortiz (HorizonBridge SRE)

Auto-generated summary: (may be imperfect) quick notes: customer cares about p95 streaming latency ~200-400ms for short responses, longer for long tokens. Interest in Dedicated for cost predictability but wants private for data residency.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
00:00 Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're Jordan at Redwood, with Avery, our systems SE. How's everyone doing?
00:08 Michael (CTO): Doing good, thanks. Sorry we're a bit late, timezone juggling.
00:12 Priya (Eng Manager): Yeah thanks for hosting, we put together some context in the invite, but want to dig into the p95 targets and how to size things.
00:20 Jordan (AE): Perfect. Quick agenda: we want to hear about your workloads, p95 targets, concurrency patterns; Avery will walk through hosting modes and how throughput/latency trade-offs look; then next steps for a pilot and benchmarks. Sound good?
00:30 Michael: Yep. To give a bit of background, HorizonBridge runs a multimodal chat assistant embedded in our logistics dashboard. We get short conversational turns, but some users do 400-800 token responses with context. Peak concurrency happens around reports refresh — bursts of 500-1200 concurrent users hitting the model for 10-30s. Steady state much lower, around 50-100. Our business target is p95 under 700ms for typical 64-token responses and we want graceful tail behavior for longer responses.
00:58 Avery (SE): Got it — that burst pattern is pretty common. One clarifying Q: are you counting p95 at the application layer (end-to-end including network + pre/post processing) or strictly the model inference time?
01:08 Michael: Ideally end-to-end, but we understand Redwood reports per-token latency. We can separate our app overhead. We mostly need to size for end-to-end SLO.
01:16 Priya: Also security — we need SOC2, SSO, KMS for keys, and audit logs. If we go private, we might need an on-prem appliance or VPC peering.
01:26 Jordan: Totally, we have SOC2 docs and KMS integrations. We'll share those after. For hosting modes: Avery?
01:32 Avery (SE): Sure. High level: Hosted is fastest to get started — multitenant, quick scaling, good for bursty unpredictable traffic but cost per token varies. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale, plus isolation. Private is our VPC/on-prem option for regulated data — same control plane but customer-managed networking and optional air-gap.
01:50 Priya: How different is latency between hosted and dedicated — is hosted throttled?
01:55 Avery: Not throttled per se. Hosted uses a pool and smart routing — you may see slightly more variance in p95 during noisy neighbor scenarios but fallback policies exist. Dedicated gives you SLOs and less variance because capacity is reserved. For example, for a 7B-ish open model serving streaming tokens, we often see 95th token latency under 80ms on Dedicated with optimized batching. Hosted might be 90–130ms depending on traffic. Those numbers are rough — we'll benchmark with your prompt mix.
02:25 Sam (SRE): Our rough budget is to keep end-to-end p95 under 700ms for 64-token responses, but we also want to understand token/sec during the burst and what concurrency maps to in terms of GPUs.
02:36 Avery: Right. We typically translate concurrency into tokens/sec and then into GPU slot counts. Two important knobs: batching and KV/prefix cache. If many requests share context, cache reduces work. If they're independent, batching helps but increases latency slightly.
02:52 Michael: For our metrics, many requests share user profile context (prefix ~1k tokens) but the new tokens per request is 40–120 tokens. So some caching applies but we still need good steady token generation.
03:06 Jordan: Can you give an example p95 target? You said 700ms end-to-end. Is there an internal p95 inference target you want us to aim for?
03:12 Michael: If you can keep model-side p95 under 250ms for the 64-token case, we should hit our end-to-end. Anything higher and our frontend will time out or feel laggy.
03:20 Avery: Understood. We'll treat that as a success criteria. For benchmarking we'll do: 1) short-turn 64 tokens, 2) mid 256 tokens, and 3) long 600–800 tokens to map tail latency and cost. We'll measure both p95 and token/sec.
03:36 Priya: What's the default batching window? We worry about added latency for real-time chat.
03:40 Avery: The runtime does continuous batching with dynamic windows — default is very small for streaming paths (tens of milliseconds) but can grow under heavy load to improve throughput. You can set latency SLOs to cap the batching window.
03:52 Michael: Question on private: if we go VPC, can Redwood still run the control plane for rollouts and telemetry? We need telemetry but can't send PII out.
03:59 Jordan: In Private mode the control plane still exists but you can choose what telemetry is forwarded; we support scrubbed logs and audit-only flows. With on-prem we can also do an air-gapped option for compliance, though that takes more lead time.
04:11 Sam: For the burst sizing, can you give a rough mapping? Say 500 concurrent users each generating 80 tokens at 15 tokens/sec average — what does that look like in tokens/sec and GPUs?
04:21 Avery: Quick math: 500 users * 80 tokens = 40k tokens in flight; at 15 tokens/sec it's 7.5k tokens/sec sustained during the burst. For a 13B model optimized/quantized on A100s — rough rule of thumb is ~8k-12k tokens/sec per GPU for generation depending on sequence length and beam size. So you'd be in the 1–2 GPU range by that metric, but engineering realities (KV cache size, concurrency overhead, streaming hooks) usually push it to 2–3 slots. We'll run your exact workload to get accurate numbers.
04:54 Michael: That mapping is helpful, but we heard from another vendor that streaming overhead kills throughput. How does Redwood handle streaming (server-sent events) and partial tokens?
05:04 Avery: Streaming is first-class — we stream tokens as they're produced. Overhead per stream is small but not zero; the main cost is kernel latency per step. Continuous batching helps amortize that cost. For very high fanout (thousands of concurrent small streams) you benefit from Dedicated with tuned batching and prefix caching.
05:26 Priya: Do you support function-calling or tool calls? Some of our flows call external APIs mid-turn which pauses generation.
05:31 Avery: Yes, function/tool calling patterns are supported. That introduces additional latency on your side for the external call; Redwood's runtime can checkpoint KV cache and resume generation quickly.
05:41 Michael: About pricing — what's the difference per token hosted vs dedicated?
05:45 Jordan: Hosted is usage-based and has a per-token rate; Dedicated is a capacity reservation with lower per-token cost at commit levels. We'll send a tailored pilot pricing sheet with an example for your expected burst profile.
05:56 Sam: On security — are audit logs immutable? We need to present to auditors.
06:00 Jordan: We support append-only audit logs with retention controls; for Private we can integrate with your logging and SIEM. We'll attach SOC2 and logging docs.
06:10 Priya: For the pilot, we'd like a controlled canary that falls back to a cheaper model if latency spikes. Is that in the platform?
06:17 Avery: Yes, rollout policies support model fallbacks and routing by latency/cost. You can set canary weights and automatic fallback triggers.
06:25 Michael: Great. Let's talk benchmarks — what's the plan and what do you need from us?
06:30 Avery: We'll need: 1) your prompt set (representative 50–100 prompts including long context), 2) a concurrency curve CSV showing burst shape, 3) a preference for hosting mode to test (we can run hosted baseline and then Dedicated sizing). We'll run token/sec and p95 tests for the three token-length buckets and return a spreadsheet mapping concurrency to GPU slots and estimated monthly cost.
06:50 Michael: We'll share those. How long to run tests?
06:52 Avery: We can do a quick baseline within 3–5 business days after we get artifacts; a full sizing including private option and on-prem estimates might be 10–14 days due to infra setup.
07:02 Jordan: For next steps, we'll send the SOC2 + KMS + private deployment docs, plus a draft pilot pricing. Avery will own the benchmark runs.
07:12 Priya: One more question — latency SLOs in your console: can we get token-level breakdown per route?
07:16 Avery: Yes, per-route and per-model token breakdowns, plus tracing hooks to correlate app-span to model-time.
07:24 Michael: Cool. Any gotchas we should know?
07:27 Avery: Two things—1) if you have long shared context and many unique users, make sure your cache/sharding strategy keeps hot KV local to workers; 2) if you expect extremely spiky fanout (10k+ concurrent short streams) plan for Dedicated with burst policies or multi-region failover.
07:46 Sam: We'll validate the concurrency numbers and share the CSV. We'll also ask procurement about budget for a 3-month pilot.
07:52 Jordan: Great — wrapping up, quick recap: Avery will run benchmarks; Jordan will send pricing and security docs; HorizonBridge will share prompts and concurrency curves.
07:59 Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
08:03 Michael: Thanks — talk soon.

(End of transcript - note: transcription may contain misheard product names like "Redwood Dedicate" or "Redwood Privatee" and some speaker labels might be generalized.)
